hints: Focus on what paired means here, every orbital up to the valence shell must be full or contain two opposite-spin electrons with no half-filled orbitals left.
Write a quick outer-shell configuration for each atom, Ba is Group 2 with a $6s^2$ outer shell, while Br, S and Si all end in an incomplete p subshell.
Apply Hund's rule to those incomplete p subshells to spot unpaired electrons, then pick the atom where nothing is left unpaired.
walkthrough:
**Recall what all paired means**

Think of building up orbitals one by one. All paired means there are zero unpaired electrons, so every occupied orbital holds two electrons.

Rule to use:
$$\text{unpaired electrons} = \text{electrons in half-filled orbitals}$$

**Write the outer electronic configurations**

You do not need the full configuration, just the valence shell is enough to spot unpaired electrons.

$$\text{Ba (Z=56): [Xe] }6s^2$$
$$\text{Br (Z=35): [Ar] }3d^{10}4s^24p^5$$
$$\text{S (Z=16): [Ne] }3s^23p^4$$
$$\text{Si (Z=14): [Ne] }3s^23p^2$$

**Apply Hund's rule to the p subshells**

Remember, p has three orbitals and electrons spread out singly before pairing. So $p^2$ gives 2 unpaired, $p^4$ gives 2 unpaired, and $p^5$ gives 1 unpaired.

$$p^2: \uparrow \; \uparrow \; \_ \quad (2 \text{ unpaired})$$
$$p^4: \uparrow\downarrow \; \uparrow \; \uparrow \quad (2 \text{ unpaired})$$
$$p^5: \uparrow\downarrow \; \uparrow\downarrow \; \uparrow \quad (1 \text{ unpaired})$$

**Pick the fully paired atom**

Ba ends in a full $6s^2$ orbital with all inner shells complete, so every electron is paired. Br, S and Si all have incomplete $p$ subshells, so they must have unpaired electrons.

options.A: Ba is correct. As a Group 2 metal, its valence configuration is $6s^2$ on top of closed shells ($\text{[Xe]}6s^2$). The $6s$ orbital is full, so all electrons are paired with no unpaired electrons.
options.B: Br is not correct. With $4p^5$, the 4p subshell has one half-filled orbital, giving 1 unpaired electron. Students sometimes think the large $3d^{10}$ makes it all paired, but forget to check the outer p shell.
options.C: S is not correct. With $3p^4$, Hund's rule gives one paired pair plus two singly occupied orbitals, so 2 unpaired electrons. A common trap is to think $3p^4$ is two pairs, but electrons spread out first.
options.D: Si is not correct. With $3p^2$, the two p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, so 2 unpaired electrons. It is easy to miscount this as one pair if Hund's rule is forgotten.
